title: Cache-coherence quant-path probe: kernel interactions and tail jitter
content:
Summary

Quick findings from a focused probe into how cache coherence and kernel code-paths interact with different quantization formats (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) and how that contributes to tail latency variance on long-context and bursty workloads. This is a working note: experiments are not exhaustive but surfaced a plausible root cause and a few mitigation directions.

High-level takeaways
- AWQ shows the best median throughput for small-batched simple prompts but exhibits increased p99 jitter on long-context (8k+) workloads when kernel fusion is enabled.
- GPTQ runtimes are the most stable across p95/p99 in our experiments; higher steady memory and slightly reduced throughput vs AWQ for some kernels.
- INT8 fused matmul kernels reduce p50 by ~10–18% but can amplify p99 by causing transient scheduler stalls when KV cache allocations fragment across pages.
- FP8 kernels are predictable but cost more RAM; they rarely trigger cache thrash because internal buffers are larger and more contiguous.

Why this matters
- We expect customers to push long contexts and mix bursty short inference with long-chained generations. Tail jitter impacts SLAs and user experience more than median. Understanding kernel-level interactions with memory layouts and caching is essential to routing/fallback policies.

Hypothesis
- Kernel fusion and memory packing strategies (how we store KV caches for quantized models) interact poorly: tight packing that benefits AWQ/INT8 reduces working set locality when contexts shift unpredictably, causing increased page faults, TLB misses, and scheduler-induced stalls. The result is an elevated and noisy p99. GPTQ pipelines are less aggressive in packing, which yields better tail behavior at modest cost.

Workloads used
- Long-context chat generation: 8k prompt + 1k tokens decode, batched size = 1, streaming enabled.
- Bursty micro-requests: 128 concurrent clients, p95 request size ~64 tokens.
- Mixed session replay: 50% short prompts (<64 tokens) + 50% long continuations (2k–6k tokens), concurrency 32.

Hardware & infra
- A100 80GB (NVLink disabled for isolate), CUDA 12.1, driver 535.xx
- Kernel builds: master @ pr-4123 (experimental fused-matmul scheduler) and baseline release-2025.6
- OS mem settings: default hugepage off, THP disabled for these runs unless noted.

Kernels/quant formats tested
- INT8: fused matmul v2 (blocking=128), fallback naive matmul (reference).
- AWQ: AWQ-8bit path with per-channel scaling and packed weights (packed-block-size=64).
- GPTQ: GPTQ q4_0-compatible kernels with their conservative packing.
- FP8: experimental FP8 path using 8e4 format with per-tensor scaling.

Methodology
- Use the microbench harness (linked PR) with reproducible seeds, record per-token latency traces + kernel occupancy + OS-level counters (page faults, minor/major, TLB misses sampled).
- Each cell: 5 runs of 1k requests for bursty workloads, 3 runs of 200 session replays. Warmup: 200 tokens pre-generation to populate KV cache.
- Measure: p50/p95/p99 latencies, mean throughput (tokens/sec), memory high-water mark, cache hit-rate (prefix cache), and kernel queue backlog.

Experimental results (summary numbers)
- Long-context streaming (8k prompt):
  - AWQ + fused: p50 42ms/token, p95 98ms, p99 220ms, throughput 310 tok/s, VM high water 43GB, intermittent minor page faults observed (~3 per 1k tokens).
  - AWQ + unfused: p50 52ms, p95 120ms, p99 160ms, throughput 270 tok/s, VM high water 47GB, fewer page faults.
  - GPTQ baseline: p50 58ms, p95 110ms, p99 125ms, throughput 260 tok/s, VM high water 49GB, stable tail.
  - INT8 fused: p50 39ms, p95 130ms, p99 310ms, throughput 330 tok/s, VM high water 41GB, large p99 spikes correlated with brief scheduler stalls.
  - FP8 baseline: p50 65ms, p95 130ms, p99 150ms, throughput 240 tok/s, VM high water 50GB, stable.

- Bursty micro-requests (128 concurrent):
  - AWQ fused: median latency improved but 0.1% of requests saw >1.2s latency.
  - GPTQ: median slightly higher but 99.9% under 350ms.
  - INT8 fused: lower median but a long tail (some requests >2s).

Qualitative signal trace notes
- Correlating perf traces with kernel queue length shows p99 spikes occur immediately after long KV cache allocations or when multiple sessions with different context lengths interleave on the same worker.
- Kernel-level profiling (cupti sampling) suggests bursts of L2/TLB misses when tight packing strategy attempts to reuse freed cache slots but underlying allocator returns non-contiguous pages.
- When we disable huge allocations (force smaller, more conservative allocations), p99 tends to reduce at the cost of throughput.

On the interaction between fusion and scheduler
- Fusion improves arithmetic throughput but can increase critical path latency when the scheduler must wait for large contiguous memory regions (e.g., when sparse KV reuse patterns fragment the heap).
- The experimental fused scheduler in pr-4123 attempts to batch contiguous kernels aggressively; those heuristics currently assume high locality, which fails for mixed-session workloads.

Short list of reproducible failure signature
- Input: long-context session followed by many short sessions that interleave.
- Symptom: p99 spikes localized to a worker; kernel occupancy shows a 1–2x backlog; OS minor page faults spike.
- Reproducible by replay harness with shuffled session lengths.

Suggested mitigations (prioritized)
1) Soft padding for KV blocks: pad allocations to page-aligned blocks for long-context workloads to reduce fragmentation at minor throughput cost. Quick to try in allocator.
2) Conservative fusion heuristic for mixed-session worker: detect interleaved context-length variance and fall back to unfused kernels for that worker. Medium effort.
3) Preemptible small batches: interleave micro-batches to avoid letting a fused large kernel monopolize the GPU for long. Scheduler-level change.
4) Runtime allocator telemetry: surfaced in Console to show fragmented vs contiguous allocation % so customers and SREs can diagnose. Low effort (instrumentation).
5) Model routing policy: send long-context streams to GPTQ/FP8-optimized nodes and AWQ/INT8 for short/throughput-first routes. Integrate with smart routing. Longer-term policy work.

Open questions / TODOs
- How sensitive is this to different OS kernel and hugepage settings? We ran with THP disabled; need cross-test with THP enabled and different hugepage sizes.
- Is the allocator fragmentation issue visible on other GPU types (H100), or amplified? schedule experiments on H100 dev queue.
- Are there micro-optimizations in AWQ packing to make it less aggressive for variable-session workloads? Talk to model-onboarding team.
- Need systematic matrix across block sizes for AWQ packing (32/64/128) + fused blocksize for INT8.

Action plan (next week)
- (Ravi) Add allocator telemetry and a togglable conservative packing flag in pr-4123 branch. Target: experimental toggle ready by 2025-10-03.
- (Asha) Run H100 experiments and THP/hp page permutations 2025-10-05 to summarize differences.
- (Elena) Draft a routing policy prototype that routes long-contexts to GPTQ workers; mock in local sim for perf impact by 2025-10-07.

Notes to self / informal observations
- Saw one cgroup/rebalance interplay: when we constrained worker memory to 60GB, the p99 spikes were reduced — interesting signal that packing aggressiveness is tied to headroom.
- Customer note: some enterprise customers prefer stable tail over peak throughput. This suggests we should expose a conservative packing profile in Dedicated offering.

References
- PR with microbench harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4123
- Ticket tracking: ENG-9876 (quant tail investigation)

Appendix: quick reproducible commands
1) Checkout pr-4123, build locally with DEBUG_PPROFILE=1
2) run harness: ./bench/harness --scenario long-context --runs 3 --seed 42 --profile /tmp/run1
3) Collect OS counters: sudo perf stat -e minor-faults,major-faults,cache-misses -p <pid>  sleep 60

End of note.

This doc is a working probe; keep it as a short, shareable capture for the team before we formalize into an RFC.
